definition: Place two pieces so their printed / 'good' faces touch. You sew on the wrong side, then turn the item so the seam is hidden.
The back face of the fabric — the side that ends up hidden inside the finished item.
The front, 'good' face of the fabric that shows on the finished item.
The distance between the cut edge of the fabric and the stitching line.
Sew 3–4 stitches in reverse and then forward again at the start and end of a seam to lock the threads.
Lift and lower the iron onto the fabric rather than sliding it, so pieces don't stretch out of shape.
A line of stitching very close (2–3 mm) to a folded edge or seam.
A visible line of stitching on the right side, usually 5–7 mm from an edge, for strength and a crisp finish.
Temporary long stitches that hold layers in place; they're hidden inside a later seam.
The direction of the threads that run parallel to the selvedge. Pieces cut on grain hang straight and don't twist.
The tightly woven finished edges running along both sides of the fabric length. They don't fray.
Place the edge of the pattern piece exactly on the folded edge of the fabric so it opens into one symmetrical piece.
Snip diagonally across the seam allowance at a corner (without cutting the stitches) so it turns out sharp.
A folded tunnel of fabric that holds elastic or a drawstring.
A stabilising layer fused or sewn to the wrong side of fabric to add body.
A cut edge of fabric that isn't finished and can fray.
Corners sewn across so a flat bag gets depth and a flat bottom.
A narrow presser foot that lets the needle sew right next to zipper teeth.
An invisible hand stitch that closes an opening from the outside.
A section of a seam left unsewn so you can turn the item right side out.
A side-to-side machine stitch used to stop raw edges fraying or to sew stretchy elastic.
Stop with the needle down in the fabric, lift the presser foot, turn the fabric, lower the foot and continue.
